summary: Lists the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Architecture Board. These periodic snapshots helped people see which protocols were standards. This edition is historic and was replaced by RFC 1880.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card showing which Internet rules are official, which are drafts, and which are just ideas. It was replaced by a newer one.

subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's periodic snapshot of which protocols are official standards.

tldr.problem: Internet developers need to know which protocols are official standards, which are still experimental, and how protocols move through the standardization process.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines maturity levels (standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, historic) and requirement levels (required, recommended, elective, limited use, not recommended), then lists all protocols in each category.
tldr.outcome: This edition (July 1995) became historic when replaced by RFC 1880; periodic updates help the community track the evolving standards landscape.

today: RFC 1800 is a Historic Internet Standard, superseded by RFC 1880. The practice of maintaining an official list of standardized protocols continues, with periodic updates reflecting the evolving state of Internet standards.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) maintains this list to help the Internet community understand which protocols have official status. The RFC describes how protocols advance through maturity levels: they start as proposed standards (on the standards track), then become draft standards, and finally reach standard status. Each advancement requires scrutiny, testing, and approval by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). At minimum, a protocol must stay proposed standard for 6 months before advancing to draft, and draft for 4 months before becoming standard.

Some protocols are experimental (for research, not operational use), informational (published for reference but outside the IESG process), or historic (superseded or no longer useful). Each protocol also has a requirement level: required (must implement), recommended, elective (optional), limited use (experimental or special circumstances), or not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols climb a ladder: first they are proposed for discussion, then they are drafted and tested, then they become official rules everyone should follow. Some rules are just experiments, some are just notes, and some are old rules nobody uses anymore.

sections.title: Maturity and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Each protocol occupies a position in a matrix defined by two independent attributes. Maturity level (or STATE) describes where a protocol stands: standard, draft standard, proposed standard, experimental, informational, or historic. Requirement level (or STATUS) describes how important it is for a system to implement it: required, recommended, elective, limited use, or not recommended.

A new protocol typically enters the standards track as a proposed standard with elective status, meaning the community is considering it for future standardization but systems are not required to implement it yet. As it gains testing and support, it may be promoted to draft standard and eventually to standard. A system must implement required protocols, should implement recommended ones, and may implement elective protocols. Some protocols, like those developed outside the IESG, are published as informational for convenience rather than as standards.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to sort protocols: first by how official they are (proposed, draft, approved, experimental, informational, or old), and second by how important they are (must have, should have, nice to have, limited use, or not recommended). A protocol could be official but elective, or experimental but important to know about.

sections.title: The Standards Track Process
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates the path a protocol takes to become a standard. Entry onto the standards track requires IESG recommendation. Once on the track, a protocol moves from proposed standard (state 1, minimum 6 months) to draft standard (state 2, minimum 4 months) to standard (state 3), with IESG approval required at each step. The diagram shows that protocols may also be assigned to experimental state (state 4) if the IESG determines the protocol is not ready for standardization, or historic state (state 5) when they are superseded or no longer useful.

The process ensures that standards are thoroughly reviewed and tested before official adoption. A protocol on the standards track goes through significant scrutiny; advancement generally requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability of two or more independent implementations. Once a protocol reaches standard status it may remain there for many years, providing stability for the Internet infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting a protocol approved is like passing through checkpoints. First it waits and gets feedback (proposed), then it gets real testing (draft), then it becomes official (standard). If it is not working out, it can stay experimental or be declared old. Each step takes at least a few months.

sections.title: The RFC Series and Document Role
sections.content:
All Internet standards are published as RFCs (Requests for Comments), but not all RFCs are standards. The RFC series is the formal record of the Internet research and development community. Anyone can submit a document for publication, but RFCs intended as standards must be approved by the IESG. The RFC series spans a wide range of documents, from meeting reports to specifications of protocols.

Once an RFC is assigned a number and published, it is never revised or reissued with the same number. If a protocol is improved, it receives a new RFC number. This ensures there is never ambiguity about which RFC version is current; the Internet Official Protocol Standards memo serves as the authoritative reference for determining which RFC contains the current specification of each protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs are the official written rules and notes for the Internet. When someone writes a new rule, it gets an RFC number and never changes. If the rule gets improved, it gets a new number. This memo tells you which RFC number has the newest version of each protocol.

sections.title: Standards Categories and Why This Document Matters
sections.content:
This memo organizes protocols into sections: standard protocols (divided into general standards and network-specific standards), draft standard protocols, proposed standard protocols, Telnet options, experimental protocols, informational protocols, historic protocols, and obsolete protocols. For each, it shows the maturity state and requirement level, allowing developers to understand the current status of any protocol.

The memo notes that RFC 1800 is itself a standard, with requirement level required, making it part of the formal specification suite. The document includes reference materials such as the Assigned Numbers (RFC 1700), Host Requirements (RFCs 1122 and 1123), and Router Requirements (RFC 1812), pointing readers to related specifications. This periodic snapshot became historic when RFC 1880 superseded it, but the practice of maintaining an official standards list continues to this day as a critical tool for the Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is like a big filing cabinet that sorts all the Internet protocols by how official they are. It tells you: this one is approved and required, that one is being tested, this old one is no longer used. It got old itself when a newer version replaced it, but new versions keep coming out.
